posts.title: Finding: some ad styles start dear and end average (check before you cut)
posts.hook: Some ads look like losers for two months, then end up average.
posts.caption:
Some ads look like losers for two months, then end up average.
Cut them in week two and you never find out which kind you had.

We looked at every new video ad launched between May and September 2026 across the brands we work with. Some ad styles started about 35% dearer per order in their first two months. Over their whole life they ended close to average.

Before you cut an ad on early cost per order, check three things:

1. Have you run this style before? Look at how it behaved over its full run last time.
2. Is the ad new, or a copy of something already live?
3. Did you write down a review date before launch?

An early number is a first reading. Give the ad the time its style has needed before.

posts.title: Festive-season maths: count your look-alikes before sale week
posts.hook: Six look-alike ads in three days: each got 48% less spend.
posts.caption:
Six look-alike ads in three days: each got 48% less spend.
That is the festive-season habit most D2C teams are about to repeat next week.

Sale weeks push teams to launch more. More sizes, more cuts, more versions of the ad that worked in October.

Our analysis of new video ads launched from May to September 2026 says the extra versions pay back poorly.

New ads that looked like many ads already running got 36% less first-month spend.

When six or more look-alikes went live within three days, each one got 48% less.

Our reading: near-copies end up sharing one budget. You pay to make six ads and get the reach of far fewer.

A count you can do before Black Friday week:

Lay every planned ad side by side as thumbnails.
Group the ones a stranger would call the same ad.
Keep the strongest one from each group and hold the rest back.
Put the saved production time into one ad that looks different.

A short launch list where every ad has a reason to exist will teach you more than a full folder.

posts.title: Before the sale: three lines that turn it into a test
posts.hook: The sale starts tomorrow. Decide today what it should teach you.
posts.caption:
The sale starts tomorrow. Decide today what it should teach you.
Most sale reports say what sold. Few say what the brand learned about its ads.

A sale is the biggest ad test most D2C brands run all year, and it usually runs without a question.

Pick one question before Black Friday goes live.

For example: at the same discount, does an ad that leads with the offer do better than an ad that leads with the product?

Then write three lines:

The question, in one sentence.
The two ads that answer it, identical except for the one thing you are testing.
What you will do in December if the first is ahead, and if the second is.

On Monday you will have revenue either way. These three lines add an answer you can brief from.

2. Put your proven message in a new look.

posts.title: Creative fatigue: the order the signals move, and refresh or cut
posts.hook: By the time cost per order moves, the ad is already tired.
posts.caption:
By the time cost per order moves, the ad is already tired.
This week it matters more than usual: the ads that carried your sale have been shown to the same people for days.

Cost per order is the last number to react. If you wait for it, you pay for the delay.

The order we check, earliest sign first:

Hook rate. Fewer people stay past the first three seconds.
Hold rate. Those who stay leave sooner.
Frequency. The same people are seeing it again and again.
Cost per order. Only now does the bill change.

Then one decision: refresh or cut.

Refresh when the hook has faded but the people who do watch still buy. The message is working and the opening is worn out. Keep the message and shoot a new first three seconds.

Cut when hook rate is steady and orders have still dropped. People are watching and choosing not to buy. A new opening will not fix that.

Look at the early numbers on Monday, before the bill tells you.

posts.title: Why we review creative every two weeks, and the four-part agenda
posts.hook: A quarterly creative review looks at ads that have already been replaced.
posts.caption:
A quarterly creative review looks at ads that have already been replaced.
A weekly one looks at ads that have not settled. We run ours every two weeks.

Two weeks is long enough for a new ad to gather data you can read, and short enough for the finding to change the next brief.

Four parts, same order every time:

Decode. What ran, and what each ad was made of: hook, cast, pacing, setting, CTA.
Prove. Which attributes moved cost per order, and which only looked good.
Create. The next briefs, written from what was proved.
Run. What to scale, what to cut, where to shift spend.

One rule: the meeting ends when the next brief has changed because of it.

You can run this from a spreadsheet. The cadence is what most teams are missing.

posts.title: Agents, not headcount: three tests before an agent decides alone
posts.hook: Before you give an AI agent a job, list your team's decisions.
posts.caption:
Before you give an AI agent a job, list your team's decisions.
Most plans list tasks, which is how the agent ends up producing reports nobody asked for.

Take one week of your marketing team's work and sort it into two columns.

Moving information: pulling numbers, renaming files, building the Monday deck, chasing a creator for a draft.

Deciding: which ad to cut, what the next brief says, whether a creator gets a second video.

In the first column an agent can take the whole job. For the second column, three tests are worth applying before an agent decides anything alone:

Can it be undone? Pausing an ad can be reversed tomorrow. A signed creator contract cannot.
Does it come up every week? Frequent decisions give you enough cases to check the agent's record.
Can it show its working? If you cannot see why it chose, you cannot correct it.

A decision that passes all three can go to the agent. The others stay with a person, and the agent prepares the evidence.

Done properly, your team gets its hours back for the second column.

posts.title: Five checks on a creator's last ten videos before you agree a fee
posts.hook: A creator can have real followers and still sell nothing for you.
posts.caption:
A creator can have real followers and still sell nothing for you.
Most shortlists check the audience. Few check the videos.

Before you agree a fee, watch the creator's last ten videos and ask:

1. Do the first three seconds give a reason to keep watching, or only a greeting?
2. Have they sold in your category or price range before?
3. On paid posts, do the comments ask about the product?
4. Do they speak your buyer's language and know their context?
5. Is there a format they repeat well, for your second video to build on?

A creator who passes four of the five is worth a paid test video. One who passes two is a guess with an invoice attached.

The audit costs you an evening. A wrong creator costs the fee and the month.

posts.title: The one-page pilot brief: five lines before any pilot starts
posts.hook: Six weeks, a tidy deck, and nobody can say if it worked.
posts.caption:
Six weeks, a tidy deck, and nobody can say if it worked.
That is how most vendor pilots end, and the cause is usually visible on day one.

A pilot that starts without a decision attached cannot finish with one.

Before any pilot begins, with us or with anyone else, put five lines on one page:

The business question. One sentence a finance head would understand.
The baseline. The number today, and the period it comes from.
The yes result. What you will see if it works, and what you buy or expand when you do.
The no result. What you will see if it does not, and what you stop.
The end date, and the one person who makes the call.

The third and fourth lines carry the page. If both results lead to the same next step, the pilot answers nothing and you can skip it.

Year end is when pilots for the new quarter get agreed. Ask every vendor for this page before the kick-off call. A vendor who resists writing down the no result has told you something useful.

posts.title: The belief we carry into 2027: ad learnings belong to the brand (the handover test)
posts.hook: When your media buyer leaves, your ad learnings usually leave too.
posts.caption:
When your media buyer leaves, your ad learnings usually leave too.
The one belief we are carrying into 2027: what a brand learns from its ads should belong to the brand.

Most D2C teams have plenty of data and no memory. The numbers sit in the ad account. The reasons sit in one person's head, an agency's deck or a WhatsApp thread.

A test for this quiet week: imagine a new hire starts on 4 January. Using only what is written down, could they brief your next ad?

For each ad that mattered, they would need four things:

What the ad was made of.
What happened when it ran.
What the team decided because of it.
Where the file is.

If that record exists, your 2026 spend bought knowledge as well as orders. If not, January starts from zero.

posts.title: AI creative needs three gates: brand, difference, learning
posts.hook: AI made ads cheap to produce. It also made look-alikes free.
posts.caption:
AI made ads cheap to produce. It also made look-alikes free.
For a D2C team using AI to multiply its creative output, the hard job has moved from making to choosing.

In our analysis of new video ads launched from May to September 2026, new ads that looked like many ads already running got 36% less first-month spend.

A generator fed on what you already ran tends to hand back more of what you already ran. Volume goes up and the account sees the same idea again.

So put three gates between the generator and the ad account.

Brand gate. With the logo covered, would a customer still recognise this as you?

Difference gate. Place it next to your live ads. If a stranger cannot tell it apart from one of them, it does not go live.

Learning gate. Write one line on what this ad will tell you that the others cannot. An ad without that line waits.

A person holds each gate. The model can prepare the evidence for all three.

An ad that gets through has a reason to exist, however it was made.

posts.hook: Three things we decided Galvor would not do.
posts.caption:
Three things we decided Galvor would not do.
It is National Startup Day, and what a company refuses to do describes it better than a feature list.

We will not touch your media budget. Our work is the creative that goes into it, and advice is easier to trust when the adviser does not control the spend.

We will not give an ad a single score. An ad is a hook, a cast, a pace, a setting and a call to action. We price each attribute against cost per order, because briefs are written attribute by attribute.

We will not hide the reasoning. Vira, our digital co-worker, shows its thinking, so a marketer can disagree with a single step.

To founders building from India today: write down what your company will not do. It explains you faster than a tagline.

posts.title: Proof (wellness): testing the category's default style, and how to set the test up
posts.hook: In wellness, aspirational content is the default. One brand tested it.
posts.caption:
In wellness, aspirational content is the default. One brand tested it.
The result is published, and the test design is yours to copy.

The numbers for this Ayurvedic supplements D2C brand (anonymised, on galvor.ai): a 2.6× uplift versus aspirational content, +135% hold rate and +91% RoAS.

This does not mean aspirational content is bad. It means every category has a default style that nobody questions, and the default deserves one fair test.

The slides show how to set that test up on your own account.

If you would like us to find the default in your category, we will decode it free. Details are in the first comment.

posts.title: AI-generated vs AI-informed: the four-line brief (keep, change, avoid, measure)
posts.hook: The best AI ad brief starts with an old ad.
posts.caption:
The best AI ad brief starts with an old ad.
Specifically, the message from the ad that has already sold for you.

Two findings from our analysis of new video ads launched from May to September 2026:

A proven message in a new look got 47% more first-month spend.
A new message over a familiar first shot got 16% less.

Most prompts run the other way. “Make ten fresh concepts for our serum” asks for new messages, and the tool tends to wrap them in the look it has seen most.

A four-line brief that follows the data:

Keep: the one promise that has sold before, in the customer's words.
Change: the first shot, the setting and the person on screen.
Avoid: describe the ads you are running now, so the tool steers away from them.
Measure: the single number that decides whether this version stays.

That is what we mean by AI-informed creative. Your own results set the brief, and the model does the making.

Use the tool for speed. Let your history choose the direction.

posts.title: Data Privacy Day: six questions before you connect your ad account
posts.hook: Six questions to ask before you connect your ad account to anything.
posts.caption:
Six questions to ask before you connect your ad account to anything.
It is Data Privacy Day, and most D2C teams grant access in one click, mid-demo.

Your ad account holds your spend, your creative and what your customers respond to. Any tool that reads it, ours included, should answer these in writing:

1. Do you need read access or manage access, and why?
2. Who inside your company can see our data?
3. Is our data used to train models or build benchmarks that other brands see?
4. If it is pooled, how is it anonymised?
5. What happens to our data when we leave, and how soon?
6. Can we see a log of what was accessed?

A good vendor has the answers ready. A slow or vague reply is an answer too.

posts.title: Label every creative finding: proven, signal or hunch
posts.hook: Most creative learnings are one ad's result with a confident name.
posts.caption:
Most creative learnings are one ad's result with a confident name.
“UGC works for us” often means one video did well in one week.

A finding from a single ad is worth keeping. It is also worth labelling honestly, because the next brief will be built on it.

Three labels cover it:

Proven. The same pattern showed up across several ads and more than one review cycle.
Signal. Seen once, or in a small sample. Worth a deliberate test.
Hunch. Someone's reading of the account, with no comparison behind it yet.

Then decide what each label is allowed to do.

A brief can lean on a proven finding without discussion. A signal gets one slot in the next batch, built to confirm it or end it. A hunch is written down with its owner's name, and is tested or dropped by the following review.

Nothing moves up a label because a senior person likes it.

After a few cycles the proven list will be short. That is normal, and it is the list to put real money behind.

The Republic Day sale has just handed you a pile of single results. Label them before you brief February.

posts.title: Ninety days of posting, reviewed like an ad account: four patterns and a review format
posts.hook: Ninety days of posting, reviewed the way we review ads.
posts.caption:
Ninety days of posting, reviewed the way we review ads.
Four patterns, what we are changing because of each, and a review format you can copy.

We tell brands that every ad should make the next one better. A content calendar deserves the same treatment, so we went through our own page and a week of public posts from companies in our space.

The patterns are in the slides.

None of this is a law. It is one page and one short window, which makes each finding a signal to test.

If you run a B2B page of your own, the review format on slide six is yours to take.

slides.headline: Ninety days of posting, *reviewed like an ad account*
slides.sub: Four patterns, and what we are changing.

slides.headline: People reach further than *pages*
slides.body:
Posts from a team member's own profile reached far more people than posts from the company page.

What we are changing: the page now backs the people on the team and stops trying to out-post them.

slides.headline: How-to posts drew more than *product posts*
slides.body:
In a week of public posts from companies in our space, posts a reader could copy the same day drew the most response. Feature announcements drew almost none.

What we are changing: one usable method in every post.

slides.headline: Templated daily series *fade fast*
slides.body:
Series that repeat one template every day drew very little response on the public pages we looked at.

What we are changing: fewer posts, each with its own argument.

slides.headline: Follower count did not predict *response*
slides.body:
Among the pages we looked at, larger ones often drew less response per post than smaller ones.

What we are changing: we judge a post by its comments and saves, and treat follower growth as a result.

slides.headline: A 90-day review for *any B2B page*
items: Sort posts by type, then compare response
Check people's profiles against the page
Name one thing to stop and one to start
Label each finding a signal until repeated

posts.title: From reporting to learning: every row of the report ends in a verb
posts.hook: A report that ends without a decision is a receipt.
posts.caption:
A report that ends without a decision is a receipt.
It proves the money was spent and says nothing about Monday.

Most weekly ad reports carry the same columns: spend, impressions, clicks, cost per order, return. All of them describe what happened.

One change turns the same report into something a team can act on. Every row must end in one of four verbs.

Scale. It is working and has room.
Cut. It has had a fair run and is not paying.
Refresh. The message sells and the look is tired.
Test. We do not know yet, and here is the ad that will tell us.

A row that cannot take a verb does not belong in the report. That alone shortens most decks.

Then add one line under the table: what we learned this fortnight that changes the next brief. If that line is blank two reports running, the team is reporting and has stopped learning.

Agencies and in-house teams can make this change without new data or new tools. The numbers stay the same and the last column is new.

From dashboards to decisions is a short trip once every row has a verb.
